blocks.title: Reaction mechanism
blocks.text: A reaction mechanism is a detailed, step-by-step description of how a chemical reaction occurs at the molecular level to yield the products. Unlike the balanced equation, which shows only reactants and products, it reveals the individual elementary steps that actually happen, each a single molecular event such as the breaking or forming of bonds.

Many reactions proceed through a series of steps rather than in one. Each step is an elementary reaction caused directly by the collision of atoms, ions or molecules, and the number of reactant molecules in an elementary step is its molecularity. A unimolecular step involves a single reactant molecule, as in the decomposition N2O5 giving NO2 + NO3; a bimolecular step involves two, as in CO + NO3 giving NO2 + CO2 or NO + O3 giving NO2 + O2; a termolecular step involves three molecules at once and is rare, as in 2O2 + O giving O3 + O2 in the stratosphere or in smog. Intermediates are short-lived species (ions or free radicals) produced in one step and consumed in a later one; they do not appear in the overall equation because they are not stable products.

In many mechanisms one step is much slower than the others: the rate-determining step, which controls the overall rate because it limits the speed at which the reaction can proceed. The overall equation is the net result of all the steps. Any step after the rate-determining step does not affect the rate, so the species taking part after it do not appear in the rate expression, while all reactants in the rate-determining step do appear in the rate equation. Because the rate-determining step limits the overall rate, the order can be deduced from it.

For 2NO(g) + 2H2(g) giving 2H2O(g) + N2(g), six experiments (Table 7.3) show that with [NO] constant, doubling [H2] doubles the rate and tripling it triples the rate, so rate is proportional to [H2]; with [H2] constant, doubling [NO] multiplies the rate by four and tripling it by nine, so rate is proportional to [NO]^2. The rate equation is rate = k [H2][NO]^2, third order, and it cannot be predicted from the balanced equation. A possible two-step mechanism: step 1 (slow, rate-determining) 2NO + H2 gives N2 + H2O2; step 2 (fast) H2O2 + H2 gives 2H2O. For 2NO2(g) + F2(g) giving 2NO2F(g) the observed rate law is rate = k [NO2][F2], first order in each and second overall; the accepted mechanism is step 1 (slow) NO2 + F2 gives NO2F + F, rate = k1 [NO2][F2], and step 2 (fast) NO2 + F gives NO2F. The first step is slow and determines the rate, in agreement with the observed rate expression; the fast second step does not affect the rate because fluorine atoms react with NO2 as soon as they are produced.

blocks.prompt: Acidified hydrogen peroxide reacts with iodide, H2O2 + 2H+ + 2I- giving 2H2O + I2, with rate = k [H2O2][I-]. The proposed mechanism is: H2O2 + I- giving H2O + IO- (slow); H+ + IO- giving HIO (fast); HIO + H+ + I- giving I2 + H2O (fast). Explain why this is consistent with the rate equation, and name the intermediates.
blocks.explanation: The slow first step is rate-determining, and it involves one H2O2 and one I-, so the rate is first order in each and independent of H+, exactly the observed rate = k [H2O2][I-]. The hydrogen ions and the second iodide enter only in the fast later steps, so they do not appear in the rate law. IO- and HIO are intermediates, made in one step and used up in the next; adding the steps gives the overall equation.

items: A mechanism is the sequence of elementary steps; molecularity is the number of molecules in one step (uni-, bi-, termolecular); intermediates are made and consumed and never appear in the overall equation.
The slowest step is rate-determining and its reactants make up the rate law: 2NO + H2 slow gives rate = k [H2][NO]^2; NO2 + F2 slow gives rate = k [NO2][F2]; later fast steps do not affect the rate.
